title: Longest Duplicate Substring
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every length with direct substring comparison versus binary searching the length and testing each with a rolling hash.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s of lowercase letters, return the longest substring that occurs at least twice in s (at different starting positions), or an empty string if no substring repeats.

blocks.text: Find the single longest substring of s that appears in at least two different places (their starting positions must differ, though the substrings themselves could technically overlap).

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Repeated Phrase in a Long Text
blocks.text: Picture searching a long document for the longest phrase that appears more than once anywhere in it, whether the two occurrences are close together or far apart.

blocks.caption: If a length-L duplicate exists, shorter duplicates exist too, enabling binary search

blocks.text: The substring "ana" appears twice (at index 1 and index 3), and is the longest such repeated substring.
No substring of any length repeats, so the answer is an empty string.

Before comparing every pair of substrings directly, notice that the existence of a duplicate substring is a MONOTONIC property in its length: if a duplicate of length L exists, a duplicate of any shorter length also exists (just take a piece of it).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The question "does a duplicate substring of length L exist" has a yes/no answer that flips at most once as L increases, from "yes" for all small L up to some maximum, to "no" beyond it.

Observation 2: This monotonic structure means binary search can find the largest L for which the answer is "yes," instead of checking every length one at a time.

Observation 3: For a fixed length L, checking every substring of that length for a duplicate can be done efficiently with a rolling hash, computing each substring's hash incrementally in O(1) per position instead of re-hashing from scratch.

Observation 4: Because hash collisions are possible (different substrings occasionally hashing to the same value), any hash match found must be verified by comparing the actual substrings before accepting it.
This leads to binary searching the answer's length, and for each candidate length, using a rolling hash to check in O(n) whether some substring of that length repeats.
Try candidate lengths from longest to shortest, and for each length, directly compare every substring of that length against every other, stopping at the first length where a duplicate is found.

items: For length L from n minus 1 down to 1, check every pair of substrings of length L for equality.
The first length where any pair matches gives the answer.
If no length has any matching pair, the answer is an empty string.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: for each length, directly compare every pair of substrings

codes.python:
def longest_dup_substring(s):
    n = len(s)
    for length in range(n - 1, 0, -1):              # try longest length first
        seen = set()
        for start in range(n - length + 1):
            sub = s[start:start + length]
            if sub in seen:                              # direct string comparison via a set
                return sub
            seen.add(sub)
    return ''

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every candidate length is checked completely, from longest to shortest, stopping only once a duplicate is actually found.
Substrings are compared directly (via a set of full strings), which itself costs O(length) per insertion or comparison.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed) in the worst case, up to n lengths, each needing O(n) substrings compared at O(n) cost per substring.
Space: O(n squared), storing many substrings, each up to length n.

Limitation: comparing full substrings directly, and checking every length one at a time from the top, is far too slow for strings up to 30000 characters; both the per-substring cost and the number of lengths checked need to shrink.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every length linearly, and comparing full substrings, is wasteful: the yes/no answer for "does a duplicate of length L exist" is monotonic in L, so binary search finds the boundary far faster than checking every length; and comparing SUBSTRINGS directly costs O(length) each, when a HASH comparison can be O(1).

What replaces full substring comparison: a rolling hash (Rabin-Karp), where sliding the window by one position updates the hash in O(1), instead of re-hashing (or re-comparing) the whole substring.

How to handle hash collisions safely: whenever two substrings' hashes match, verify they are ACTUALLY equal before accepting the match, since different substrings can rarely collide to the same hash value.

The core idea: binary search the candidate length; for each candidate, slide a rolling hash across the string once, checking a hash-based set for repeats (verified against collisions), to test that length in O(n).

Binary search on the duplicate length L, from 1 to n minus 1. For each candidate L, compute a rolling hash for every length-L substring in a single O(n) pass, checking a hashmap for a repeated hash value (verifying the actual substrings match, to rule out collisions). If a duplicate is found at length L, remember it and try a longer length; otherwise, try a shorter one.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search the length, verify with a rolling hash each time

blocks.text: Binary search correctly narrows in on the longest working length because the property is monotonic: any length shorter than a working length also works. For each candidate length, the rolling hash lets every substring's hash be computed in O(1) from the previous one, so the entire length is tested in O(n); verifying actual equality on a hash match guards against the rare case of two different substrings colliding to the same hash value.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) expected, a binary search over O(log n) lengths, each tested in O(n) with the rolling hash.
Space: O(n) for the hash map at each tested length.

blocks.text: This is a textbook combination of two techniques: binary searching a monotonic property (the existence of a duplicate at a given length) and a rolling hash (Rabin-Karp) to test each candidate length efficiently, with collision verification to keep the result correct.

items: Forgetting to verify an actual substring match on a hash collision, which can silently produce a wrong (too-long or nonexistent) answer.
Recomputing each substring's hash from scratch instead of updating it incrementally as the window slides.
Using a single hash modulus that is too small, or a hashing scheme prone to frequent collisions on adversarial inputs.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating the monotonic property first, "if a duplicate of length L exists, shorter duplicates exist too", is the key justification for binary search, and mentioning collision verification shows awareness of a subtle correctness pitfall.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "checking every length is slow", think: the existence of a duplicate is monotonic in length, binary search it.
If the interviewer says "how do you avoid comparing full substrings", think: a rolling hash, verified against collisions on a match.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n cubed) time and O(n squared) space. The optimized binary-search-plus-rolling-hash approach runs in O(n log n) expected time and O(n) space.

items: Pattern: binary search on a monotonic property (duplicate existence at a given length), tested with a rolling hash.
Core Idea: binary search the longest length at which a duplicate substring exists; test each candidate length in O(n) using a rolling hash, verifying any hash match against actual substring equality.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n log n) expected for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: duplicate existence is monotonic in substring length, enabling binary search instead of checking every length.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known hard problem; correctly combining binary search, rolling hash updates, and collision verification is the full challenge.
One line memory trick: binary search the length, Rabin-Karp hash to test it, verify on any match.
